title: Solving the teacher shortage
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Responding to news that 499 Australian school leavers with ATARs under 50 were offered teaching places, Brien questions whether lowering entry barriers is a sensible answer to a teacher shortage. He argues the shortage is overstated, noting roughly 100,000 qualified teachers not deployed in schools, and that high out-of-field teaching and weak university preparation are bigger problems. He ties retention to workload, burnout and the loss of mid-career teachers, and suggests that shared planning and checks for understanding in place of marking could free time. The second half turns satirical, offering five admittedly unhinged proposals: backpacker teacher visas, a relief-teaching lottery like jury duty, full funding, paid overtime and a sports-style trade season. The humour is a vehicle for a serious point about pay, workload and respect for the profession, though the body of statistical support is thin and mostly footnoted links.
points: Brien challenges the premise of a shortage by pointing to about 100,000 qualified teachers who are not working in schools.
He argues lowering entry requirements sets pre-service teachers up for failure and debt, and pushes schools to re-teach misconceptions from graduates.
Workload is the retention lever he returns to, citing 12 hours of unpaid weekly overtime and mid-career burnout.
Shared planning and checks for understanding are offered as ways teachers can reduce the workload they create for themselves.
quotes: Even the idea that there is a teacher shortage is overblown. According to AITSL there are 515,000 qualified teachers in Australian, however only 81% are deployed in schools which means there are almost 100,000 qualified teachers available but potentially unwilling to step back into the classroom.
Yet our solution to this shortage is to hop in the excavator of our more highly paid friends in the trades5 and dig a huge pit to drop the bar into now that it’s been set so low.

If we truly want to improve student outcomes and therefore improve student opportunities, should we not invest in the teachers we currently have and set the high expectations we’d expect of our students to our pre-service teachers.

Further to all of these points is that schools are struggling having to re-teach graduate teachers to correct any misconceptions that have been developed or to build knowledge that was never created in the first place around best practice such as Multi-tiered Systems of Support.7 This further adds to the extreme workload of new career teachers who are often working 2 to 3 hours additional to more experienced teachers which can then put them on the fast track to burning out.
If we are smarter in our shared planning and using checks for understanding to replace taking worksheets away to mark teachers free up countless hours.

Australian public school teachers work on average 12 hours of unpaid overtime per week. Effectively reducing their own salary by almost one third. Imagine the change in teacher retention if teachers were paid for this overtime.

Long have we considered it to be our civic duty to be involved in jury duty. Long have we also considered the general public to not understand the plight of the school teacher. So how about alongside the lottery for jury duty, all registered voters are drawn at random to need to report to CRT for two weeks within their catchment zone. Suddenly the wider public appreciates the work that a teacher does day in and day out.
